newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada firms duel for control of Venezuela gold.
newsitem.headline: Canada firms duel for control of Venezuela gold.

text.p: An ownership dispute over Placer Dome Inc.'s Las Cristinas gold project in Venezuela heated up on Thursday, raising doubts about whether the company can start building a $576 million mine there next month as planned.

Investors were bewildered by conflicting accounts of a Venezuelan court ruling given by Placer and Crystallex International Corp., the small Vancouver company that has laid claim to the two richest blocks of the Las Cristinas property.
Crystallex said on Thursday that the Supreme Court of Venezuela earlier this week issued a ruling that "reaffirms Crystallex's position as to the validity of its ownership rights" of the blocks.
But Placer said its title to the property was secure and that the court ruling dealt only with procedural issues that had no bearing on its tenure.
Vancouver-based Placer has 70 percent of the project in southeastern Venezuela and its joint venture partner, Venezuelan's state-owned mining concern CVG, the rest.

The dispute has swirled since February when Crystallex said it acquired rights to the concessions by acquiring a company, Inversora Mael CA, that previously owned the property. Then, as now, Placer and Venezuelan officials vehemently disputed Crystallex's contention.

Venezuela Mines Minister Erwin Arrieta repeated on Thursday the government's belief that Placer had title to the property. "There is no legal problem," he told reporters in Caracas. "...Our legal advice has been that Placer is the concessionaire."

Most analysts said they were betting on Placer at this stage, but several said they were increasingly nervous about the dispute. They said investors had become more skittish after recent control battles over other high-profile mineral properties such as Voisey's Bay in Canada and Busang in Indonesia.

"I think Placer Dome is more persuasive, but I'm pretty confused. I don't know what to make of this. The thought that this could blow up in Placer's face is pretty scary," said one analyst, who asked not to be identified.

Investor jitters were apparent on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Thursday where shares of both Placer and Crystallex were among the most heavily traded. Placer was down C5 cents to C$23 after earlier falling to C$2.20. Crystallex fell C22 cents to C$3.79 after trading in a range of C$3.55 to C$4.30.
Las Cristinas is a key part of Placer's growth plan. It had planned to start building a mine there next month that would ultimately produce 450,000 ounces of gold a year.
The project experienced a delay earlier this year as Placer and CVG sought to iron out details of their contract. Placer is now seeking final permits and financing for the mine.
One Wall Street analyst said the latest development made it appear unlikely that Placer could break ground in May. "I'm not sure that's (going to be) reality," he said.

But he predicted that Placer would ultimately prevail, although it might require further court battles or an out-of-court settlement. "My view is that when this is finally adjudicated you will see Placer being the victor," he said.

Analyst Dorothy Atkinson of Whalen Beliveau in Vancouver sided with Crystallex. "Crystallex seems to have a very good case for ownership," she said, adding that she found Placer's explanations of the situation unsatisfying.
Placer acquired Las Cristinas in 1991 through a contract with the Venezuelan government.
